query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the as-cast non-equilibrium microstructure contains metastable, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that, on exposure to high-temperature or corrosive environments, transform into stable intermetallic phases. This transformation promotes the segregation of Mg to surfaces and grain boundaries, in turn fostering the formation of a coherent, protective Mg-rich oxide (or passivation) layer that modifies subsequent corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, metastable high-entropy alloy with a density below 6 g/cm³, consisting of a predominantly solid solution matrix containing dispersed, metastable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to controlled high-temperature aging or corrosive (e.g., saline) environments to induce the transformation of metastable Mg-rich intermetallics into more stable phases.
generation.conditions: Testing under high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 600–800°C) and/or in a saline corrosion environment, compared to an as-cast baseline microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution (phase transformation) of metastable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates into stable intermetallic compounds, along with the segregation of Mg at critical microstructural sites (grain boundaries/surfaces).
generation.mechanism: The transformation alters the local chemical potentials and interfacial energy, enabling a continuous, adherent Mg-rich oxide or passivation layer to form. This layer, in turn, shifts the dominant electrochemical and oxidation reactions, thereby modifying the corrosion rate and high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to the original metastable state.
generation.predicted_outcome: After exposure, the alloy will display a changed phase composition with increased stable Mg-rich intermetallic content and the formation of a coherent, protective oxide layer. Relative to the as-cast baseline, these evolved samples are predicted to exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (evidenced by lower weight gains or uniform oxide scales) and a measurable shift in corrosion potentials and/or reduced corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: The as-cast microstructure with a high density of metastable, nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallics, which lacks the protective oxide scale that develops upon phase transformation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold only for lightweight high-entropy alloys designed to remain below 6 g/cm³ and may not apply if the initial degree of Mg segregation or distribution of metastable phases is significantly different. Additionally, excessive environmental severity might disrupt the formation or continuity of the protective layer.
generation.uncertainty: The kinetics of the intermetallic transformation and the detailed structure and adherence of the resulting oxide layer are not fully established, leaving some uncertainty regarding the balance between improved oxidation resistance and any potential embrittlement or loss in other mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical alloy samples, keeping one set as-cast (baseline) and subjecting the other set to controlled high-temperature aging and/or saline corrosion tests. Characterize the microstructure and surface composition before and after exposure using techniques such as XRD, TEM, and XPS. Perform electrochemical corrosion tests and high-temperature oxidation measurements (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis) to compare performances.
measurements: Phase composition and crystallinity via XRD and TEM
Surface chemistry and oxide layer characterization via XPS/EDS
Corrosion rates and potential shifts via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization
Weight change and oxide scale uniformity during high-temperature oxidation via TGA and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged/co-exposed samples do not show a significant transformation in the Mg-rich intermetallic phase content or fail to develop a coherent, protective Mg-rich oxide/passivation layer—and if the corrosion and oxidation performance does not significantly differ from the as-cast baseline (or degrades unexpectedly)—then the hypothesis is falsified.
